extracted.intended_audience: readers of military history / students of Napoleonic campaigns / general readers of memoirs
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards implied or stated in a soldier's memoir for judging the quality of command, troop behaviour, tactics, and campaign outcomes during the Peninsular War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallantry measured by casualties when holding/advancing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The surest criterion by which to judge of the gallantry and steadiness of the Spaniards during those operations is by reference to the casualties they suffered.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial guidance: while losses alone can be ambiguous (a body may suffer loss while running away), when men are advancing or standing still and yet suffer severe loss, that is a reliable proof of bravery and firmness. Example/interpretation: high casualties sustained while fighting forward = evidence of steadiness and gallantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership competence: vigilance and preparedness of generals
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Soult ‘loudly complained of want of vigilance in his generals; and not without just cause, for they were nowhere prepared.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: commanders are judged by readiness and vigilance; failure to prepare or remain vigilant is a legitimate cause for reproach and can change battle outcomes. Implied scoring note: preparedness of subordinate commanders reduces risk of surprise and failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deception and manoeuvre to conceal intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated praise for Wellington’s and allied manoeuvring: ‘Everything was so well arranged that not the slightest appearance of an attack was discovered.’ Soult’s confused-looking movements were ‘designedly so, with a view of deceiving Wellington.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical criterion: successful deception and false attacks (feints, manoeuvring camps, leaving tents standing) that conceal the true point of attack are judged positively. Example: the false attacks that held D’Erlon’s attention allowed the main crossing to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and decision to hold or retreat (operational judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection that ‘had Picton with the two divisions under his command continued to retreat for two hours longer ... Soult would inevitably have gained the double object which he had in view.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational standard: timely halting and positioning can prevent enemy objectives; premature or over-hasty retreat can concede critical strategic advantages. Assess commanders on whether they halted/held at decisive moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentry vigilance protocols and enforcement (stone-chatters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of sentry protocol: the usual cry ‘All’s well’ was replaced by ‘stone chatters’—stones struck twice in slow time; if a sentry neglected this for more than five minutes the next struck thrice quickly and a piquet visit followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard for camp security: regular audible signals with built-in escalation detect sleeping/negligent sentries. Guidance includes timing (every five minutes) and escalation behaviour (three quick strikes triggers a visit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline in interactions with the enemy (no parley/contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: ‘It was prohibited under the heaviest penalty that soldiers should ever exchange a word with the enemy.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary standard: strict prohibition on informal communication with proximate enemy posts; maintaining strict rules of engagement preserves order and security. Also notes occasional informal exchanges at officer level were practiced but formally forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of provisioning and pay on troop reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: ‘the army was very scantily provisioned; and many disgraceful desertions took place to the French who were well supplied.’ Also soldiers were six months in arrear of pay, affecting behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistics criterion: adequacy of supplies and timely pay strongly influences desertion rates, morale, and reliability. Assessors should consider provisioning as key to unit effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of reorganising/remodelling after defeats
rubrics_metrics.description: Soult ‘immediately set about remodelling his army; and to revive their confidence and rouse their drooping spirits ... he determined to make an offensive movement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Command standard: after setbacks, effective reorganisation and decisive offensive action can restore morale and combat effectiveness. Guidance: reorganisation + visible offensive operations are positive indicators of recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and cooperation of allied forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for the Spaniards and Portuguese fighting ‘with the greatest bravery’ and note that Spanish divisions were ‘intermixed with those of the British’ aiding performance compared with earlier campaigns where they were held aloof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coalition criterion: close operational integration of allied contingents (intermixing units, shared lines) is judged positively; contrasts with prior poor arrangements where allies were separated or poorly commanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconnaissance and use of maps for operational decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wellington ‘hurried to Echallar to reconnoitre the enemy and consult his maps,’ an act that nearly led to his capture but demonstrates the role of reconnaissance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: active reconnaissance and map consultation are necessary to inform command decisions; personal reconnaissance by commanders is a sign of sound operational practice (but also carries personal risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of feints/false attacks to fix enemy forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated accounts of the 6th Division’s false attack on D’Erlon deterring him from reinforcing other sectors and enabling the true attack’s success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical metric: employment of diversionary attacks that successfully fix or distract enemy reinforcements is an effective tactic and should be credited in evaluations of campaign planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of historical description requires multiple narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Author admits inability to provide full description because ‘the information necessary to furnish accurate detail must depend on the narratives of many.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historiographical standard: accurate reconstruction of complex multi-corps actions requires collating many accounts; single-officer memoirs are inherently partial. Guidance: prefer multi-source synthesis for reliable detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct toward civilian populations after storming
rubrics_metrics.description: After San Sebastian’s storming ‘the town was set fire to in all quarters; and the most shocking barbarities ... were perpetrated by the British soldiers on the unfortunate inhabitants.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical/disciplinary criterion: maintenance of troop discipline towards civilians after assaults is a crucial measure of command control and moral conduct. Such atrocities are condemned and mark a severe lapse in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering/fortification as a defensive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that the enemy ‘were incessant in fortifying their lines from the base of the mountains to their very summit, upon which their strong forts and redoubts were constructed.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational standard: the construction and use of fieldworks, forts, and redoubts to dominate terrain is a key defensive measure; assessors should note the extent and effectiveness of fortifications when judging defensive performance.
